01 · About

A little about how I work

I'm a self-taught UI/UX designer and fresher, with hands-on experience in Figma, wireframing, prototyping and user-centred design. My path started with a Bachelor's in Computer Applications, where I picked up an interest in how software actually gets used, and design became the natural next step.

I care about clarity over decoration: every screen starts from a real user problem, worked through with user flows, wireframes and interactive prototypes before a single pixel is "final." I'm eager to contribute and grow inside a collaborative design team.

Case Study

APEPDCL Electricity App Redesign

The current APEPDCL app makes something as simple as checking or paying a bill harder than it should be. This redesign makes it clearer, simpler and easier for everyone, including elderly users.

Role
UX/UI Designer
Tools
Figma, FigJam
Goals
Usability, accessibility, navigation
Open in Figma →
The Problem

The existing app packs everything (Add Service, Bill Pay, Customer Care, Consumption, Connect, Payment History, Link Aadhaar, My Usage, Supply Position) into one crowded grid, with no clear priority given to Pay Bill, the app's main purpose. Paying a bill takes unnecessary extra steps, the UI feels outdated, and several features repeat across sections instead of living in one place.

Research

Target users: residents, bill payers, and elderly consumers. Talking through their pain points surfaced four recurring issues:

01

Confusing navigation

Users must search through multiple sections to perform simple actions like bill payment.

02

No clear primary action

The home screen doesn't highlight Pay Bill, increasing decision time and effort.

03

Poor readability

Small font sizes and low contrast make the app hard to use for elderly users and low vision.

04

Too many payment steps

The payment process includes unnecessary steps that add friction and confusion.

A quick competitive read against TGSPDCL, the neighbouring utility's app, confirmed the direction. APEPDCL's pay-without-login option and 12-month usage insights were real strengths worth keeping, while TGSPDCL's clearer primary bill-payment access was worth borrowing.

Before

Everything carries equal visual weight; the outstanding bill is nowhere on screen.

After

The outstanding bill, a Pay Now action and the consumption trend sit above the fold.

Before

Bill reminders are written as full paragraphs, repeated per service number.

After

Alerts are grouped into scannable cards by day, with a direct Pay Now action.

Before

The receipt reads like a printed slip, with contact numbers and fine print mixed in.

After

Transaction and bill details are broken into scannable label and value rows.

Before

Checking a complaint means entering a number into a bare form with no visible history.

After

A step-by-step tracker shows exactly where a complaint stands, with an estimated resolution time.

Information architecture

The original IA was flat and repetitive: nine near-equal top-level sections, several leading to near-identical destinations (My Usage, Consumption and Supply Position all showed variations of the same data). I restructured it around four jobs: Home (bill status and quick actions), Pay Bill, Customer Care (complaints, tracked end to end) and More (account, language, Aadhaar, settings), all reachable from a persistent bottom tab bar instead of a single scrolling grid.

UI design decisions

I sketched low-fidelity wireframes first to test the new structure, then built the visual system in Figma:

Primary Blue #2E4898
Secondary Blue #D5E8FC
Success Green #10B981
Error Red #EF4444

Typeset in Inter throughout, for its clean legibility across small mobile screens, directly addressing the readability pain point from research.

The flow, end to end
Log in
Home
Pay bill
Confirmation
Track complaint
Outcome

The redesign turns a 9-icon decision into a single glance: the outstanding bill, a primary action and the consumption trend are visible the moment the app opens. Faster bill payments, a cleaner dashboard and a more modern interface were the headline wins. Because it was designed with accessibility in mind from the start, elderly users can complete a payment independently, without the confusion the original flow caused. This was an independent redesign exercise, not a shipped release, and the full screen set and prototype are viewable in Figma.
